fields.meta_title: Invoice Approval Workflow Built on Your Rules | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Set up an invoice approval workflow from four routing rules: split invoices, discount deadlines, changed bank details, and self-approval blocks.
fields.h1: Build an Invoice Approval Workflow Around Who Approves What
fields.hero_description: Build an invoice approval workflow that sends each invoice to the right approver, chases late sign-offs, and logs every decision.
fields.features_heading: The Rules Behind Every Invoice Sign-Off
fields.features_subheading: Emergent builds your approval policy as an app: who signs at each amount, what is checked first, and who gets reminded.
fields.feature_1:
Approval limits by amount and cost center

Each approver gets a dollar limit, and each cost center gets an owner. An invoice goes first to the owner of its cost center, then up the chain until an approver's limit covers it.
fields.feature_2:
PO invoices checked before approval

An invoice that quotes a PO number is compared with the PO and the goods receipt. Prices and quantities inside your tolerance pass; a mismatch goes to the buyer named on the PO.
fields.feature_3:
Decisions from Slack, email, or the app

Approvers see the invoice, its coding, and the PO in one message, with approve and reject buttons. A rejection needs a reason, and the invoice returns to AP with the reason on it.
fields.feature_4:
Reminders timed to the due date

Choose how many days before the due date an approval must land. An approver who misses that mark gets a reminder, and one more day of silence moves the invoice to their manager.
fields.feature_5:
A decision log in a database you own

Every approval, rejection, reroute, and reminder is saved with the person and the time. Auditors read each invoice's history from your own database, not a vendor's export screen.
fields.feature_6:
Your approval rules as code in GitHub

Export the app's full code, limits and holds included, to your GitHub repository on paid plans. A developer can review each routing rule as code before it changes how invoices move.

fields.tab_content_1:
Two budget owners split one $8,400 invoice

Kittredge Events bills $8,400 for a customer summit on INV-5528, coded $5,040 to Sales and $3,360 to Marketing. Each share goes to its budget owner at the same time. Henrike Mbatha has approved the Sales share: 1 of 2 approvals is in. The invoice waits for Joaquim Ferrante to approve the Marketing share.
fields.tab_content_2:
The $252 discount gets a reminder on day 7

Fenmore Packaging's INV-90412 for $12,600 offers a 2% discount if paid within 10 days, worth $252. The app sets the approval due 3 days before the discount ends, on day 7. Rosalind Ikeda has not decided by then. She gets a direct message in Slack with the $252 at stake and an Approve button.
fields.tab_content_3:
New bank details hold the invoice for the controller

Corvay Freight's INV-3307 for $2,975 names a payment account ending 4410, and the vendor record has one ending 0318. The invoice is held, whatever its amount, for the controller, Dariusz Achterberg. It goes on to its approver only after he calls Corvay at the phone number on file and marks the change verified.
fields.tab_content_4:
Nobody signs off on an invoice for their own order

Zainab Albrecht ordered a $1,480 sales course from Pinewick Learning, and INV-7716 is coded to the cost center she owns. As its owner, she would be the approver. The app skips her because she placed the order and sends the invoice to her manager, Benedikt Amadi.

fields.howto_title: How to Create an Invoice Approval Workflow
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to set up an invoice approval workflow that routes every invoice by your own rules, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Write each rule as one sentence
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Name one owner and one backup
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Count back from the payment run
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pull last quarter's invoices and note who approved each one and how many days it waited. The gaps show up quickly: invoices nobody owned, approvers with no limit, and vendors paid before anyone signed off.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Describe each rule the way you would explain it to a new AP clerk: marketing invoices go to the marketing budget owner, and anything above that owner's limit goes on to the controller. Emergent builds the app, its database, and the routing from those sentences.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Give every cost center a single owner and a named backup for vacations and leave. An invoice with two possible owners stalls while each waits for the other, and one with no backup stalls for the length of a vacation.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Pick each approval deadline by counting back from your payment runs. If runs go out on Thursdays, an invoice due on a Friday needs its approval by Thursday morning, or it misses the run that pays it on time.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Connect QuickBooks, Xero, or NetSuite through its API so approved invoices post with their coding. Read vendor records from the same system. The bank details the app compares against are then the ones finance keeps up to date.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Run last month's invoices through the rules before any live invoice does. Check that each one reached the approver you expected and that every split invoice reached all of its owners. Change a rule by prompting, then run the month again.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Once live, read the decision log at each month end. Look for approvers who keep missing their deadline and limits that send too many invoices to the controller, then change the rule behind each one.

faq_plan.a: An invoice approval workflow is a chain of sign-offs that a supplier bill clears before anyone pays it. It sets who signs off on each bill, in what order and under what rules, and where a disputed or escalated bill goes next.

faq_plan.q: How do I create an invoice approval workflow?
faq_plan.a: Write your rules down as plain sentences first: who owns each cost center, and how much each approver may sign for. Then describe them to Emergent's AI automation builder. Emergent builds the approval app and its database from that prompt, and you change a rule later by prompting again.

faq_plan.q: What should invoice approval workflow software do?
faq_plan.a: It should send each invoice to the person who owns its budget, hold it there until that person decides, and keep the decision on record. Then look at how invoices get in. If AP still types each one by hand, the software routes faster than the work arrives.

faq_plan.q: Is a payment approval workflow separate from invoice approval?
faq_plan.a: No. Invoice approval confirms that a bill is owed and coded correctly; a payment approval workflow then picks which approved invoices go out in a payment run, and on what date. Give those two decisions to different people. A contract behind the invoice can clear a document approval workflow of its own before the first bill arrives.

faq_plan.q: How many approvers should an AP approval workflow have?
faq_plan.a: Plan on one approver for invoices inside the budget owner's limit and two above it: the budget owner, then the controller. Add a third only where leadership asks to see the spend, such as a new vendor's first invoice. Each added approver adds a wait. An app built with Emergent has no per-approver seats, and the chain can follow your controls instead of a license count.

faq_plan.q: Which steps of an invoice approval workflow should a finance team automate first?
faq_plan.hint: How to automate invoice approval workflow finance team?
faq_plan.a: Automate the handoffs first and leave the judgment with people. Nobody on the team needs to carry an invoice to its approver or chase a late answer by hand. Deciding whether a charge is fair stays with the budget owner. The app Emergent builds can also read each invoice into fields with AI and send any field it is unsure of to a person.

faq_plan.q: How is an invoice approval workflow different from other sign-off processes?
faq_plan.hint: How to automate invoice approval workflow?
faq_plan.a: Two things set it apart: an amount and a due date. A content approval workflow can wait a day for a better draft, but an invoice that sits past its due date can cost a late fee or an early-payment discount. The amount also decides who may approve it. Every route needs a dollar limit and a deadline.

faq_plan.q: How should an invoice approval workflow handle invoices with no PO?
faq_plan.hint: What to use for invoice approval workflows in scf?
faq_plan.a: Send it to the owner of the cost center it is coded to, after AP confirms the coding. With no PO, there is nothing to match the price against, and the budget owner is the only check on it. Ask vendors who bill often to quote a PO number on every invoice, and the number of these exceptions drops.

faq_plan.q: How can an invoice approval workflow flag duplicate invoices?
faq_plan.hint: Which expense management platforms automate invoice approval workflows?
faq_plan.a: Have the workflow compare each new invoice with the ones already logged for that vendor, by invoice number and amount. Any match waits for AP before it reaches an approver. Check near matches too, such as the same amount a few days apart, since a resent invoice can carry a new number.

faq_plan.q: What should an approver check in an invoice approval workflow before signing off?
faq_plan.a: Check that the goods or the service arrived, then that the price matches what was agreed. The coding comes last: is it the right cost center for the spend? A reject with a reason sends the invoice back faster than a question in a side thread. Requests that carry no invoice, such as travel or software purchases, can run through a general approval workflow instead.

findings.quote: Ramp and Brex both do, in their bill pay products. Ramp routes bill approvals on conditions such as amount, vendor name, and accounting category, and Brex can route bills for approval by amount and vendor. With Emergent, every budget owner can approve invoices without a per-approver seat.
findings.issue: The moat line sits directly after the two named platforms, so it reads as the edge over Ramp and Brex. That edge is false on their entry plans: Ramp's Free plan is '$0/mo/user' and lists 'Configurable approval workflows' under Accounts Payable (ramp.com/pricing); Brex Essentials is '$0 user/month' with 'Multi-level approval flows' in bill pay (brex.com/pricing). It is the exact row #8 pattern ('No per-approver seats' as the edge over a vendor that also charges no per-user fee), uses brands outside the competitor library as a comparison, and breaks the F9 rule 'never branded or competitor-comparison phrasing'. Only instance of this class on the page: why_description says 'no per-approver seats' but names no competitor and the table has no seats row.
findings.fix: Keep the two cited facts and replace the last sentence with an approved moat that implies nothing about Ramp or Brex, e.g. 'An approval app built with Emergent keeps every decision in a database you own.' (database-owned), or drop the moat here and keep F9 at items 3 and 5.

findings.quote: Emergent can build the step that sends that file through the bank's API.
findings.issue: The quoted Wells Fargo span says only 'buyer approves invoices for payment and sends an approved invoice file to Wells Fargo' (the page adds 'Using existing buyer process'); it names no API, and no domain_sources entry says the bank takes the file through an API. Supplier finance programs commonly take this file by portal upload or host-to-host transfer. The sentence states a third-party system fact its source does not say. No other instance: the other Wells Fargo, Ramp and Brex sentences stay inside their spans.
findings.fix: Stay inside the span and the payments-out claim: 'Emergent can build the step that generates that approved invoice file from the decisions in your log.'
